71.title: Two sets of cousins
71.hook: cousins under one roof, two claims to one throne, and the question of dharma
71.carry: dharma is what holds the house up
71.howItsDone: Hindus know the Mahabharata through family retellings, comic books, television serials and temple recitations; tradition names the sage Vyasa as its author and Ganesha as the scribe who wrote it down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharata handed back the sandals, Rama was crowned, and Hanuman stayed. Hanuman listens wherever Rama's story is told.

Cousins who grew up together. Then something breaks between two sides of the family, and now at weddings they sit at opposite ends of the room. The Ramayana was about one family and an enemy outside it. The other great epic, the Mahabharata, is about a family where the enemy is inside. Remember Ganesha breaking his tusk to keep writing? Tradition says this is the book he was writing. This week, the cliffhangers.
screen: `COUSINS AT OPPOSITE ENDS.` → `THE ENEMY IS INSIDE.` → `THE BOOK GANESHA WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Two brothers. The elder, Dhritarashtra, was born blind, so by the rules of the time he was passed over for the throne. The younger, Pandu, became king. Pandu's five sons are the Pandavas. Yudhishthira, the eldest, so honest it becomes a problem. Bhima, huge, hungry and strong. Arjuna, the archer. And the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Dhritarashtra and his wife Gandhari, who bound her own eyes with a cloth for life so she'd never see more than her husband, have a hundred sons, the Kauravas. The eldest is Duryodhana. Then Pandu dies young, and his five boys come to live in the palace at Hastinapura with their hundred cousins. It goes bad early. Duryodhana's jealousy becomes hatred. He poisons Bhima and throws him into a river; Bhima survives. When people start calling Yudhishthira the heir, Duryodhana talks his father into sending the Pandavas away, to a house built of lac and other things that burn, meant to be set alight with them inside. Warned in time, they dig a tunnel, set the fire themselves, and slip away. Whose throne is it? Duryodhana is the son of the elder brother, now on the throne. Yudhishthira is the eldest son of the king who reigned. Both have a case. Neither lets go. This is why the Mahabharata matters so much to Hindus. Its real subject is dharma: the right way to live, your duty to the people around you. The word comes from a root meaning to hold up. Dharma is what holds a family, a kingdom, a world together. And the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, is called Dharmaraja, the king of dharma. The epic doesn't only ask who gets the throne. It asks: what is dharma here, when both sides have a claim?
screen: `THE BLIND ELDER, THE YOUNGER KING.` · `FIVE PANDAVAS, A HUNDRED KAURAVAS.` · `WHOSE THRONE IS IT?` · `DHARMA: WHAT HOLDS IT ALL UP.`

segments.voice: Think of a split in a family you know, two sides that used to share a table. Instead of asking who's right, ask the Mahabharata's question: what would dharma ask of me here, in my place in this family? If you pray, hold both sides before God, by name, without picking a winner.

72.title: The dice
72.hook: the king of dharma keeps his rule and stakes his kingdom, his brothers, his wife
72.carry: keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma
72.howItsDone: The dice game in the Sabha Parva is retold in homes, classical dance and theater, and readers often point to it as the moment the great war became hard to stop.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandava, the five sons of Pandu, raised with a hundred cousins and one throne. Dharma is what holds the house up.

Just one more hand. One more bet to win back what you lost on the last one. The Pandavas have done well. They've built a shining city of their own, Indraprastha, with a hall so magical that Duryodhana, visiting, mistakes a floor for a pool and a pool for a floor, and falls in, and people laugh. He goes home burning. His uncle Shakuni has an idea. Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, can't refuse a challenge. And Shakuni is a master of the dice.
screen: `JUST ONE MORE.` → `DURYODHANA FALLS IN THE POOL.` → `SHAKUNI, MASTER OF THE DICE.`

segments.voice: The invitation comes: a friendly game in the great hall at Hastinapura. Yudhishthira knows it's a trap. He says so, and goes anyway, because a king of his kind doesn't refuse a challenge. Shakuni throws for Duryodhana. In the popular telling his dice are loaded; the text simply says he's a master of deceit at the game. Yudhishthira stakes a jewel and loses. Gold. Chariots. His army. His treasury. His whole kingdom. Each time, he's sure the next throw will turn it. Then Shakuni asks: what else do you have? Yudhishthira stakes his brothers. The twins first, then Arjuna, then Bhima. He loses every one. He stakes himself, and loses. The hall is silent. There's one stake you haven't played, says Shakuni: your wife. And Yudhishthira, the man known for never lying, the son of dharma himself, stakes Draupadi. The dice fall. Vidura, the king's wise half-brother, has begged them all to stop the game, and no one listens. The other elders, the grandfather Bhishma, the teacher Drona, the blind king, let it go on. Look at who's playing: not a fool, but Dharmaraja, the king of dharma. Never refuse a challenge: that was his rule, and he kept it, all the way down. Many teachers read the scene this way: Yudhishthira kept the rule and lost what the rule was for. A king's dharma is to protect the people in his care, and he staked them, one by one. In that reading, dharma is bigger than any one rule: it's what the rules are there to protect. Tomorrow, what happened to Draupadi in that hall.
screen: `HE KNOWS IT'S A TRAP. HE GOES.` · `HIS BROTHERS. HIMSELF. HIS WIFE.` · `VIDURA BEGS. NO ONE LISTENS.` · `HE KEPT THE RULE, LOST ITS POINT.`

segments.voice: Think of a rule you hold tight: never back down, never ask for help, never be the one to call first. Ask what Yudhishthira forgot to ask: what is this rule for? Who is it meant to protect? If keeping it is starting to cost those very people, it isn't dharma anymore. If you pray, ask for the sense to tell the difference.
The dice. A rigged game, and a wise man who staked everything, one throw at a time.
Your line: keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma. He kept his, and lost his family. See you tomorrow.

73.title: Draupadi's sari
73.hook: Draupadi's question, and the cloth that wouldn't end
73.carry: krishna answers the one who calls
73.howItsDone: Draupadi's disrobing and the unending cloth are retold again and again in dance, theater and devotional song; devotees see in it Krishna's protection of those who call on him, and in parts of south India Draupadi herself is worshiped as a goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dice, and the king of dharma who kept his rule, one throw at a time. Keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma.

Draupadi isn't even in the hall. She's in the women's rooms when a servant comes to tell her she's been lost in a game she wasn't playing: she now belongs to the Kauravas, and must come. Instead of coming, she sends back a question. It's a sharp question, and nobody in that hall, not the kings, not the elders, can answer it. This is a hard scene, about a woman humiliated in public, so i'll tell it carefully.
screen: `LOST IN A GAME SHE WASN'T PLAYING.` → `SHE SENDS BACK A QUESTION.` → `A HARD SCENE, TOLD CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Her question: when Yudhishthira staked me, had he already lost himself? If he had, he was a slave, and what right does a slave have to stake anyone? Duryodhana doesn't answer. He sends his brother Dushasana, who drags her into the hall by her hair. Before the whole court, Draupadi asks again. The grandfather Bhishma, the elder everyone looks to, says the ways of dharma are subtle, and he can't say. Only one of the hundred Kaurava brothers, the young Vikarna, stands up and says she's right, and he's shouted down. Dushasana is ordered to strip her, in front of everyone. He grabs the end of her garment and pulls. And pulls. The cloth keeps coming, yard after yard, until Dushasana collapses, exhausted, and Draupadi is still standing, still covered. In the popular telling, she has called on Krishna, and he answers her with cloth that never ends. In a version many devotees love, she holds her sari tight at first, and only when she lets go and raises both hands to call him does the cloth start to flow. That's why this scene sits at the heart of bhakti, loving devotion: when the elders fail and no hand in the hall will help, the one who calls on God isn't left alone. The one who was supposed to be shamed is the one left standing. Bhima swears a terrible vow of revenge. Jackals howl, a bad omen. The blind king, frightened, finally offers Draupadi wishes, and she uses them to free her husbands. Her question was never answered. Her dignity was never removed.
screen: `HAD HE ALREADY LOST HIMSELF?` · `THE ELDERS CAN'T ANSWER.` · `SHE CALLS ON KRISHNA.` · `THE CLOTH KEEPS COMING.`

segments.voice: Sit with your spine straight, the way Draupadi stood. Remember a time no one in the room would speak up for you. Draupadi's answer, in the telling devotees love, was to call a name. Many Hindus still do: Krishna, Govinda, Ram, whispered in a waiting room or before a hard phone call. If you pray, say the name you pray to, slowly, three times, and hand over what you can't hold. If you don't, name one person who'd stand with you.

74.title: Thirteen years
74.hook: the yaksha's questions, a brother chosen for fairness, the year in hiding
74.carry: dharma is fair even when it costs you
74.howItsDone: The Yaksha's questions to Yudhishthira are often retold and taught as a dialogue on dharma, and the Virata Parva, the book of the year in hiding, is traditionally recited in some regions to pray for rain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Draupadi's sari, the cloth that wouldn't end. Krishna answers the one who calls.

You'd think, after all that, the Pandavas would never touch dice again. Freed by Draupadi's wishes, they head home, and they're called back. One more game, one throw. The loser goes into the forest for twelve years, then spends a thirteenth year in hiding, somewhere in the world, undiscovered. If anyone recognizes them that year, they start all over again. Yudhishthira plays. Yudhishthira loses. And five royal brothers and a queen walk into the forest with nothing.
screen: `CALLED BACK FOR ONE MORE THROW.` → `TWELVE YEARS, THEN ONE UNSEEN.` → `HE LOSES. INTO THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: The twelve forest years fill a huge part of the Mahabharata: sages, pilgrimages, stories inside stories. Near the end of them, the brothers, desperately thirsty, find a lake guarded by a spirit, a yaksha, who says: answer my questions before you drink. One by one, four brothers drink anyway and fall dead. Yudhishthira stops and answers. The questions come fast. What is the greatest wonder in the world? His answer, roughly: every day people die all around us, and the rest of us live as if we never will. He answers so well that the yaksha offers him a gift: one of your brothers may live. Choose. Bhima, the strongest? Arjuna, the great archer, the one you'll need in a war? Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, one of the twins. Why him? Because the twins had a different mother, Madri. Yudhishthira's own mother, Kunti, still has a living son: him. Let Madri have one too. The yaksha is so moved that he gives all four back, and reveals who he really is: Dharma himself, the god of dharma and Yudhishthira's own father, testing his son. That's the teaching under the scene. Dharma isn't only being right. It's being fair, even to the other side of the family, even when it costs you your best warrior. Then the thirteenth year. They hide at the court of a king called Virata, each as the last thing you'd expect: Yudhishthira as the king's dice companion, mighty Bhima as a cook, Arjuna as Brihannala, a dance teacher, and Draupadi as a maid to the queen. The year runs out, and they're not caught.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS AT THE LAKE.` · `HE CHOOSES THE OTHER MOTHER'S SON.` · `DHARMA HIMSELF, TESTING HIM.` · `THE YEAR IN HIDING AT VIRATA'S COURT.`

segments.voice: Think of a split you're part of: two sides of a family, two friends, two groups at work. Picture someone on the other side who stands to lose something too, the one who'll be hurt if it all stays broken. Ask Yudhishthira's question: what would be fair to them, not only to me? If you pray, pray for them by name. Don't decide anything yet; just let their side be real.
Thirteen years. Twelve in the forest, and one in hiding, in plain sight, at a king's court.

75.title: Krishna the negotiator
75.hook: five villages; Duryodhana refuses a needle's point of land
75.carry: even krishna asked for peace first
75.howItsDone: Krishna's peace mission, the Udyoga Parva's embassy, is told in Mahabharata recitations and dance dramas such as Kathakali, and 'not a needle's point of land' is still quoted for stubborn refusal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thirteen years, and a king who chose fairness over strength at the lake. Dharma is fair even when it costs you.

The thirteen years are over. The Pandavas kept every term of the bet, and now they want their kingdom back. Duryodhana says no. Both sides start gathering armies from every kingdom in the land. One person tries, one last time, to stop the war: Krishna. Cousin to the Pandavas, friend to Arjuna, and, for his devotees, God himself on earth. He goes to Hastinapura as an envoy of peace. And making peace between two people who both think they're right means going back and forth, shrinking the ask, looking for the smallest thing that lets everyone save face.
screen: `THE TERMS WERE KEPT.` → `KRISHNA GOES FOR PEACE.` → `SHRINKING THE ASK.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana prepares a feast to win him over. Krishna refuses it and eats instead at the house of Vidura, the king's wise and humble half-brother. A small, telling choice. Then he stands in the great hall, before the blind king, the elders and Duryodhana, and speaks for peace. Give the Pandavas their half of the kingdom. Behind that ask sits a smaller one, which Yudhishthira has already sent, and which some retellings put in Krishna's mouth in the hall: give us five villages. Just five, one for each brother, and there will be no war. Kings who once ruled a shining city, after thirteen years of exile, asking for five villages. Duryodhana answers. In the story, he won't give them even as much land as can be pierced by the point of a needle. Not without a war. His own parents beg him. The elders beg him. He walks out of the hall, and even plots to seize Krishna. In the tradition, Krishna reveals himself in that moment, showing the court a vast, blazing form filled with gods and worlds, so bright that only a few can look. Then he leaves. The war is coming. Look at who did the asking. For his devotees, this is God on earth, who could end the war with a look, and he walks into his enemy's hall and asks for five villages. Many teachers draw the lesson from it: in dharma, peace is asked for first, and humbly, before any fight can be right.
screen: `THE FEAST REFUSED; VIDURA'S TABLE.` · `HALF THE KINGDOM. THEN FIVE VILLAGES.` · `NOT A NEEDLE'S POINT OF LAND.` · `GOD CAME ASKING FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: Think of a conflict in your life that's stuck. Before you plan how to win it, do what Krishna did: look for its five villages, the smallest fair ask that could let it move. One message. One apology. Letting someone be right about one thing. If you pray, ask for the humility Krishna showed in that hall. Don't send anything yet; just find the five villages, and hold them.
Needle's point, the scrap of land Duryodhana wouldn't give. Krishna the envoy asked for half a kingdom, then five villages, and got not even that.
Your line: even Krishna asked for peace first. Five villages, and still refused. See you tomorrow, on the eve.

76.title: The eve
76.hook: both armies camped; the conch shells; Arjuna's hands shake
76.carry: the gita begins with arjuna's despair
76.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita, which opens on this scene, is recited daily by many Hindus, often chapter by chapter; the conch shell is still blown in temples and homes at the start of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: needle's point, the land Duryodhana wouldn't give. Even Krishna asked for peace first.

The night before something big. The exam, the surgery, the wedding, all playing in your head while you lie awake. A wide plain in north India, called Kurukshetra. Two vast armies camped on it, the story says: kings from every corner of the land, elephants, chariots, horses, foot soldiers stretching to the horizon. Tomorrow cousins fight cousins. Far away in the palace, the blind king Dhritarashtra can't see any of it. So he asks his charioteer, Sanjaya, who has been given the gift of seeing the battlefield from afar, to tell him what's happening.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `KURUKSHETRA: TWO ARMIES.` → `THE BLIND KING ASKS.`

segments.voice: His question is the very first line of the Bhagavad Gita. In Sanskrit it begins: dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah. On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight: what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Notice what he calls it: not just a battlefield, a field of dharma. Sanjaya tells him. The grandfather Bhishma, commander of the Kaurava army, blows his conch shell, a sound like a lion's roar. The other side answers. Krishna, who has agreed to drive Arjuna's chariot, lifts his conch, named Panchajanya. Arjuna blows his, Devadatta, the god-given. Conch after conch, until the sound shakes the sky and the earth. Then Arjuna says to Krishna: drive my chariot out between the two armies; I want to see who I'm fighting. Krishna drives into the empty space in the middle, and Arjuna looks. On the other side he sees his grandfather Bhishma, who raised him. His teacher Drona, who taught him to shoot. His uncles, his cousins, his friends' sons. And the great archer starts to shake. In the Gita's words, as closely as i can put them: his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns, his hair stands on end, and his great bow slips from his hand. He sits down in the chariot. And here's the surprise. Tradition titles this first chapter of the Gita the yoga of Arjuna's despair. Even the breakdown counts as part of the path. Krishna's teaching doesn't begin when Arjuna is brave; it begins when he admits he can't go on.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` · `DRIVE ME BETWEEN THE ARMIES.` · `THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.` · `CHAPTER ONE: ARJUNA'S DESPAIR.`

segments.voice: Notice your hands, calm or restless, and think of something you're on the eve of: a conversation, a hard day tomorrow. If Arjuna's feeling is there, the dry mouth, the heavy limbs, don't push it away; in the Gita, despair is the first chapter, not the last. If you pray, tell God plainly what you can't do, the way Arjuna told Krishna. Then breathe, slow in, slower out; you don't have to be ready yet.
The eve. Two armies on the field of dharma, the conches sounding, and a great archer with shaking hands.
Your line: the Gita begins with Arjuna's despair. He sits in the chariot, and Krishna is about to speak. That's day seventy-six.

77.title: Krishna takes the reins
77.hook: Arjuna chooses Krishna, unarmed, over a whole army, and asks him to drive
77.carry: bhakti: choosing god over the army
77.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
77.howItsDone: Hindus also call Krishna Parthasarathi, Arjuna's charioteer, and the image of Krishna holding the reins while Arjuna listens is a familiar one in Hindu homes, in temples and on the covers of the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eve, and Arjuna's bow slipping from his hand. The Gita begins with Arjuna's despair.

Before the war, before the conches, there's a scene the Mahabharata tells almost like a joke. Arjuna and Duryodhana both go to Krishna to ask for his help in the coming war. Krishna is asleep. Duryodhana arrives first and sits proudly by his head. Arjuna comes in and sits quietly at his feet. Krishna wakes, and the first person he sees is Arjuna. So he makes an offer. On one side, my whole army, a vast force of warriors. On the other, me, alone, and I won't lift a weapon in the war. Choose.
screen: `TWO COUSINS AT KRISHNA'S BED.` → `ONE AT HIS HEAD, ONE AT HIS FEET.` → `MY ARMY, OR ME, UNARMED.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, asked first, chooses Krishna. No army, just him, unarmed. Duryodhana can hardly believe his luck: he gets the army. Then Arjuna asks Krishna for one thing: drive my chariot. So the one the Gita will reveal as God becomes a driver, a sarathi, the one who holds the reins. Look at the choice. Duryodhana counted soldiers. Arjuna chose the presence of God, even a God who promised not to fight. Many devotees read this choice as the heart of bhakti, loving devotion, one of Hinduism's great paths: what matters most isn't how much power is on your side, but whether God is with you. Krishna is still called Parthasarathi, the charioteer of Arjuna, and there are temples to him by that name. You'll see the picture on home altars and on the covers of the Gita: Krishna holding the reins, Arjuna listening. For many devotees it's a prayer without words: you drive. And that's where this long run of stories pauses. A boy made of earth at a door. A leap across the sea. Sandals on a throne. A row of lamps. Cousins, dice, a cloth that wouldn't end, five villages, and a frightened man in a chariot. When someone mentions Hanuman now, or Draupadi, or Bharata's sandals, you won't nod politely. You'll know them, and what they teach. Next come the practices these stories were pointing at all along. And when a festival's date arrives, its story comes first.
screen: `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA: DRIVE MY CHARIOT.` · `BHAKTI: CHOOSING GOD OVER THE ARMY.` · `PARTHASARATHI, ON HOME ALTARS.` · `YOU KNOW THESE PEOPLE NOW.`

segments.voice: Picture a chariot, and Krishna holding the reins. Then picture something in your life that feels like a battlefield right now. Ask honestly: am I counting soldiers, or asking who's with me? If you pray, offer the reins: say, in your own words, you drive. If you don't, name what steadies you when your hands shake. Then let a few faces walk past: Ganesha, Hanuman, Sita, Draupadi, Arjuna. Notice which one stops and looks at you.
The driver. Sarathi, the one who holds the reins: Krishna, choosing to drive Arjuna's chariot instead of fighting.
Your line: bhakti, choosing God over the army. Arjuna chose Krishna, and asked him to drive. See you tomorrow.
